summary: This note presents interviews with financial aid officers Susan Moretti and David Liu (Oct 15, 2023) about how adult learners can find and win financial aid and scholarships. They stress that the FAFSA has no age limit, that many scholarships target adults, and that meeting deadlines, staying organized, and looking at employer and demographic-specific aid are key. An HR manager and two adult learners add employer-sponsored and real-life perspectives.
one_line: Financial aid officers advise adult learners on FAFSA, scholarships, employer programs, and avoiding pitfalls when funding a return to education.
key_facts: Susan Moretti (lead financial aid officer, Metropolitan Community College) and David Liu (director of financial aid, Riverside Technical Institute) were interviewed on October 15, 2023.
David Liu says many adult learners don't know they qualify for the same federal aid as younger students, since the FAFSA has no age limit.
Susan Moretti says the traditional college age is typically 18-24, and adult learners often balance work, family, and study.
The FAFSA is the entry point for federal aid and for many institutional scholarships.

Susan Moretti's checklist: get documents in order including tax returns, research deadlines that differ from traditional ones, and look into scholarships for demographics such as veterans, single parents, or first-generation students.
Veterans can use programs like the Post-9/11 GI Bill and the Yellow Ribbon Program, according to David Liu.
A common pitfall is thinking loans are the only option; David Liu notes there is a lot of 'free' money in scholarships.
Susan Moretti advises meeting all deadlines and asking questions, since each missed deadline or unasked question is potentially lost funding.
David Liu recommends using scholarship databases plus local community organizations and employers; Susan Moretti recommends keeping a spreadsheet of opportunities, requirements, and deadlines.
John Kramer, HR manager at TechVisions, was contacted on November 8, 2023; TechVisions is known for a robust education reimbursement program.
Riverside Technical Institute recently launched a 'Fast Track Scholarship' supporting adult learners in accelerated programs.
Marina Cortez, a 37-year-old single mother, said single-parent scholarships covered a significant portion of her tuition.
Joe Hammond, a 52-year-old veteran, said the GI Bill transformed his post-service life and made returning to school possible.
